bodyMarkdown:
## How to Calculate a Boilermaker Salary from an Hourly Rate

If you're a boilermaker or hiring one, understanding how an hourly rate translates into an annual salary is essential. The standard formula is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For full-time employees under most modern awards, the ordinary hours are 38 per week. So a boilermaker earning $40 per hour would have an annual salary of $40 × 38 × 52 = $79,040 before tax and super.

This calculation assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It gives you a baseline figure to compare job offers or budget your finances. You can also work out your fortnightly pay by doubling the weekly amount: $40 per hour × 38 hours = $1,520 per week, or $3,040 per fortnight.

Our [timesheet](/) lets you enter your base hourly rate and instantly see your annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures. If you're a casual employee, tick the casual loading checkbox to add 25% on top.

## Award Rates and the National Minimum Wage

Boilermakers are typically covered by the Manufacturing and Associated Industries and Occupations Award 2020, though some may fall under other awards depending on the industry. The Fair Work Commission publishes classification rates in its Modern Awards Pay Database, which includes minimum wages, allowances, and penalty rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) with easy-to-read tables for each award.

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Award rates are higher – for example, a Level 3 boilermaker under the Manufacturing Award might earn around $30 to $35 per hour, depending on experience and location. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult average weekly earnings were $2,083.70 in May 2026, which equates to about $54.83 per hour for a 38-hour week. This figure includes all occupations, so skilled trades like boilermaking often sit below that average but above the minimum.

To find the exact rate for your classification, check the [reference tables](/data) on our site or use the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay and Conditions Tool. Remember that these are minimum rates – many boilermakers negotiate above-award pay.

## Casual Loading and Superannuation

If you work as a casual boilermaker, you're entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. This loading compensates for not receiving paid sick leave or annual leave. For example, if the award rate is $32 per hour, the casual rate becomes $40 per hour. When calculating your annual salary, use the loaded rate in the formula.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. This means if your annual salary is $80,000, your employer must contribute an additional $9,600 into your super fund. Super is not deducted from your pay – it's an extra cost for the employer. Our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page explains how this affects your total remuneration.

For casual employees, super is calculated on the loaded rate. So a casual boilermaker earning $40 per hour (including loading) would have super calculated on that amount.

## Tax and Medicare Levy on Your Annual Figure

Once you have your annual gross salary, you need to estimate your take-home pay after tax. The 2026–27 resident tax rates are:

- Nil on income up to $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, most residents pay a 2% Medicare levy. For example, a boilermaker earning $79,040 per year would pay:
- $0 on the first $18,200
- 15% on $26,800 ($18,201–$45,000) = $4,020
- 30% on $34,040 ($45,001–$79,040) = $10,212
- Total tax = $14,232
- Medicare levy = 2% of $79,040 = $1,580.80
- Total tax and Medicare = $15,812.80
- Take-home pay = $79,040 – $15,812.80 = $63,227.20 per year, or about $1,216 per week.

Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator does this automatically. Note that this estimate uses the full tax-free threshold and does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. It's a guide only.

## Using the Timesheet for Your Boilermaker Salary

The easiest way to see your numbers is to use our [timesheet](/). Enter your base hourly rate – never include casual loading in the rate you type; instead, check the casual loading box if applicable. The tool will calculate your annual salary, fortnightly pay, and weekly pay. It also shows estimated tax and super.

Remember that the annual figure is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold and the 2025–26 Medicare reduction thresholds (as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this guide).

For a more precise estimate tailored to your situation, consult a tax professional or use the ATO's online tools. The Fair Work Ombudsman and Fair Work Commission are the authoritative sources for award rates and conditions.

## Other Factors That Affect Your Boilermaker Salary

Your actual take-home pay may differ due to:
- Overtime and penalty rates (e.g., weekends, public holidays)
- Allowances (e.g., tool allowance, height allowance)
- Salary sacrificing (e.g., for a car or additional super)
- The Medicare levy surcharge if you don't have private hospital cover and earn above a threshold
- HELP or HECS debt repayments

Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) and [average pay](/topics/average-pay) pages provide more context for comparing salaries across industries. For boilermakers specifically, the [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page lists typical rates by state and experience level.

Whether you're negotiating a new role or planning your budget, understanding how a boilermaker salary is built from an hourly rate gives you confidence. Start with the base rate, add casual loading if applicable, multiply by 38 hours and 52 weeks, then apply tax and super. Use our tools to see the numbers in seconds.
